<reason>Side A wins a high-level, competitive debate by proving that localized wellhead depletion justifies targeted permitting and caps rather than a geography-blind universal ban. Through pointed questioning and rebuttal, A forced B to defend banning extraction even in abundant aquifers where pumping stays within recharge, successfully framing the ban as overbroad and reliant on a speculative theory that removing bottled water will force politicians to fix failing municipal pipes. Side B mounted a very clever offensive in the later rounds by trapping A between its warning about takings litigation and its support for regulatory caps. However, A adequately distinguished conditional and prospective regulation from total expropriation, and decisively dismantled B's shifting attempt to replace private emergency bottling networks with taxpayer-funded continuous packaging. Both sides incurred minor execution costs—a clipped final word for A in Turn 4 and nonexistent reference IDs (C/P prefixes) for B in Turns 7 and 9—leaving A ahead on the core policy comparison.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's dismantling of B's emergency supply replacement across [A2.6] and [A4.3]-[A4.4] was the most effective sequence: A exposed that governments cannot "contract existing logistics networks" [B2.6] if a commercial ban closes those plants, and when B pivoted to paying operators a flat fee for continuous public packaging [B3.2, B4.2], A showed this merely shifts the full cost of standby capacity, plants, and distribution risk onto taxpayers while still relying on private operators. Side B's pressure question in [B3.1] and follow-up in [B5.2]—using A's own takings argument to attack A's regulatory model—was a close runner-up.</best_rebuttal>
